pr_body:
Internal nodes are nodes that aren't exposed to the user. This is useful for control nodes that use other control nodes and we don't want anyone to meddle with them (e.g. ColorPicker or WindowDialog).

Compared to normal nodes:

- you can't normally access them with `get_child()` or `get_children()`
- `get_child_count()` will not count internal nodes, `get_position_in_node()` will return
position - internals size
- `move_child()`'s position will skip these nodes too
- you can however access them by passing `false` to `skip_internal` argument of aforementioned methods
- `skip_internal` is `true` by default in bindings (i.e. scripts), but it's false in code (so anything relying on children indexes won't break)
- internal nodes are always at the beginning of children list, even when added after normal nodes

This is supposed to fix #30381, close #21458 and resolve #7142
(also fixes #52146, but the issue might as well get a dedicated PR)

It's probably also useful for ppl making plugins. You can make a node internal by passing `true` to the new third argument of `add_child()`.

~~This is still WIP. While implementation is ok, internal nodes should be added to other controls (right now it's only ColorPicker) and it needs doc update.~~
pr_comments: Perhaps an interesting tidbit: Last i tried the internal nodes of GraphEdit show up in the scene tree, and can be modified. (Like hiding them to prevent users from changing the zoom settings.) But this also totally breaks GraphEdit.

I played around with this after looking at the issues linked in the OP.  

As mentioned in the OP, they are not supposed to be meddled with.  They are **vital** for their parent Node type (RTL, WindowDialog, etc) to _function_.  Should Godot crash? No, but I think those are specific cases that need to be dealt with. 

 A developer can simply create a node and use it as a container to put their nodes in. Then `queue_free` the children in there. That is.. If they really want to loop through the children and remove them.  The developer can also call `queue_free` on the parent node, and it will not cause the crash.

The developer can also use [leezh's example](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/7142#issuecomment-261756979). 

Also, some GUI Nodes it's quite obvious they have internal nodes. (RichTextLabel's scrollbar in the editor)

Maybe an option to toggle the internal nodes in the editor node list could help. The real solution though  IMO, is for Godot not to silently crash when an internal node is free'd.  Not sure how to fix that, since they are not supposed to be free'd. Other people might have a better solution, though

I'm, personally, against this. Internal nodes are still nodes and their access should be the same as any other node. You can already distinguish internal nodes from other nothes because those internal nodes' `owner` property will be `null`

 I think this is more of a documentation issue. 

If anything, the only modification I'd do is to change `Node.get_children()` to `Node.get_children(with_internal_children = false)` and only return nodes with an `owner` property if `with_internal_children` is `true`.
Nodes added at runtime do not have an owner. It must be set manually.

> If anything, the only modification I'd do is to change Node.get_children() to Node.get_children(with_internal_children = false)

Actually, it could be `true` by default and `false` in bindings (if that's possible).

> The real solution though IMO, is for Godot not to silently crash when an internal node is free'd.

That means null checks everywhere the crash might happen. It would negatively impact performance (not much, but still) and failed nodes are useless anyways.

The idea of this PR is to make some nodes less obvious to access and more importantly - impossible to access accidentally, which only leads to confusion and unexpected behavior.

I just pushed a commit that added `skip_internal` parameter to (hopefully) all methods that use node indexes. In code it's `false` by default and in bindings it's `true`.

Here's a tiny project for comparison of how `get_children` etc. behaves with ColorPicker:
[ColorPickerTest.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/3365786/ColorPickerTest.zip)
Try it with 3.1 and this PR.

What's left to do is:
- add internals to other Controls that should use them
- update docs

I'm against completely hiding these, as it would mean hiding functionality from the user. If implemented, there should definitely be some kind of "get_child_unsafe" method or something.

It might be a better idea to allow users to see these nodes in the editor, which would mean that adding a node would generate its children, instead of generating them when the project is run. Maybe.

> Turns out it's not straight-forward to use this option, because many nodes rely on accessing children, like Containers and stuff. Sooo, I thought of 2 ways to solve this:

For nodes with fixed children, would it be better to store a pointer to said child node, or connecting the nodes together with signals, so that it doesn't rely on getting children?

> I'm against completely hiding these, as it would mean hiding functionality from the user. If implemented, there should definitely be some kind of "get_child_unsafe" method or something.

Yeah, that's why I made it "hidden by default" with my last commit. The `skip_internal` argument allows you to access these nodes when set to `false`. I'll edit PR description to mention this.

> It might be a better idea to allow users to see these nodes in the editor, which would mean that adding a node would generate its children, instead of generating them when the project is run.

ColorPicker has 7 internal children. I don't think it's a good idea to show them in editor. There's also _zero_ need to edit them normally.

> For nodes with fixed children, would it be better to store a pointer to said child node, or connecting the nodes together with signals, so that it doesn't rely on getting children?

But it wasn't about nodes with fixed children. Container doesn't know what you put in it beforehand. Well of course, we could tell it explicitly what nodes it has underneath or it could remember them after doing `add_child`, but that sounds more complicated to work with.

> But it wasn't about nodes with fixed children. 

What I mean is how ColorPicker has 7 internal children. AFAIK these don't change.

The thing is, ColorPicker already stores pointers to them and its internal logic is perfectly fine (that's how you should use internal nodes; you don't need to access them even from the node that use them). But it's also a BoxContainer (to keep its layout) and we would have to change the Container implementation to support "fixed nodes". Not sure if it's worth the effort and it's not really relevant to the PR, as you need to do something about these nodes either way (and I remind that right now you can access them totally accidentally and crash your app, which is not desired probably).

I updated the docs and added internal node usage to `WindowDialog`, `AcceptDialog`, `FileDialog`, `GradientEdit`, `GraphEdit`, `ItemList`, `LineEdit`, `MenuButton`, `OptionButton`, `PopupMenu`, `RichTextLabel`, `ScrollContainer`, `Spinbox`, `TabContainer`, `TextEdit` and `Tree` (they were all relying on hidden nodes and potentially had the same unexpected problems). Marking this as ready for review. I'll squash the commits when it gets approved.

While searching for solution for internal nodes, I was expecting that some of the children could be made "private". This way, when I switch `editable_children` on an instanced scene, only those which are "public" would be editable and shown. Use case:

![editable_internal_private](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/17108460/64773784-a5af9a80-d55b-11e9-887e-a892fcc6eda0.png)

In this case, I'd like to hide `points` node as it's only used internally to store spawn positions, but I'd still like to modify `start` and `end` positions which essentially define the spawn rectangle.

While I completely support this PR as a solution for my own issue #38714, I'm still concerned about silent crashes. Can the crashes at least be "loud", leave some trace behind? If something is trying to access a freed instance, wouldn't there be an error? Is it simply suppressed?

Alternatively, what if `remove_child` or `queue_free` or both don't work on nodes marked as `internal` by default and require an optional argument to be passed that would force them to work? That way you wouldn't be able to accidentally cause a crash and would have to think about the call you are making. But, I guess, it would complicate things a lot internally.
I rebased the PR, hopefully everything still works 🙃

If you don't mind me suggesting, could there perhaps be a way for a GDScript user to check if a node is marked as "internal"? Perhaps a `Node.internal: bool` property, or `Node.is_internal() -> bool` function?

I also think such a "internal" setting might be useful to expose to the Editor Inspector. But that's just me.
A meta data field would probably suffice, the editor already uses those for things like these.

> I also think such a "internal" setting might be useful to expose to the Editor Inspector. But that's just me.

The thing is that internal nodes don't show up in the scene tree (unless remote), so it wouldn't be useful.

`is_internal()` method would be easy to add.

~~I am not happy with this solution because the problem is not clear. For the most part you can check whether a node is owned or not while editing or opening a loaded scene and this should be enough. If the problem sums up to "i am going around nodes that I may have added myself and I am not sure if I added them myself" then the problem is definitely not clear.~~

I did not realize the flip in the flag for users and scripting, at first I thought it was weird but understanding the usage context it makes full sense and solves all the problems I was thinking of, so I agree with this PR. Asked for some changes though.

@reduz One big problem that this PR solves is the implementation of things like godotengine/godot-proposals#2514. Nodes (be it from the engine itself or made by others) that rely on children being added to then, but also have nodes themselves would become much more easier to implement this way.

I pushed some changes. There is now distinction between "front" internal nodes and "back" internal nodes. I removed `internal_nodes` list as it wasn't really used. The internal nodes still need to be on the main list for everything else to work, so it was only some weird "mirror" and I only used the size of that list. Instead, now Node has two variables: `internal_children_front` and `internal_children_back`. They are modified whenever internal node is added or removed. Anything with index below `internal_children_front` is considered "front internal node", and analogously with the other variable. Instead of boolean, `add_child()` now uses an integer. Less than 0 means "front internal node", greater than 0 means "back internal node".

Now this all sounds very confusing, but luckily a regular user will almost never need to use the internal nodes (outside core, it's maybe useful for plugins), so GDScript API isn't any more complex than before. But internally, Node needs to make sure that a child doesn't move beyond its expected index (i.e. if node is "front internal child", it can't be moved past `internal_children_front` index and opposite - regular node can't be moved before this index, otherwise things won't work as expected. It won't crash though, so at least there's that)

Also I changed `skip_internal` parameters to `include_internal`.

The PR still needs rebase, testing, doc update etc. so I'm putting it as draft for now.

> Instead, now Node has two variables: `internal_children_front` and `internal_children_back`. They are modified whenever internal node is added or removed. Anything with index below `internal_children_front` is considered "front internal node", and analogously with the other variable.

I'd say these names are misleading. Just by looking at them I'd think there's a single sequence of internal children where `internal_children_front` points at the first internal child and `internal_children_back` points at the last internal child. But it's actually the opposite, children in range <`internal_children_front`, `internal_children_back`> are non-internal.



> Instead of boolean, `add_child()` now uses an integer. Less than 0 means "front internal node", greater than 0 means "back internal node".

Wouldn't an enum be better?

Finally, after going through index hell and fixing infinite number of bugs, I think I got it right. I tried to test it thoroughly, but there might be some cases where something breaks (e.g. node appears at wrong index or leaves it's "internal bounds" producing unexpected results). Hopefully everything is fine though.

> I'd say these names are misleading. Just by looking at them I'd think there's a single sequence of internal children where internal_children_front points at the first internal child and internal_children_back points at the last internal child.

I need to somehow keep track of how many internal nodes of each type are there, so the indices can't change. They could be renamed though, but the name I used makes sense I think.

> Wouldn't an enum be better?

I could make an enum. I asked reduz if int is fine and he said yes, but maybe he misunderstood, idk.

EDIT:
Also I added internal nodes to all controls that need them. But some of them have to be front, some back, so there is possibility I could mess something. Also there might be non-Control nodes that use internals, but I'm not aware of any.

> I need to somehow keep track of how many internal nodes of each type are there, so the indices can't change. They could be renamed though, but the name I used makes sense I think.

@KoBeWi I've actually misunderstood what `internal_children_back` is (now I've looked at the code :smile:). I thought it's an index and `internal_children_back == size() - internal_children_back_count` since you've said:
> Anything with index below `internal_children_front` is considered "front internal node", and analogously with the other variable.

But it's actually the count of back internal nodes.
Anyway, since these variables are used only internally (!) in the `Node` their names aren't that important so they're probably fine as they are. On the other hand, for the same reason, longer names shouldn't be a problem. Thus I'd change them to something like `internal_children_count_front`, `internal_children_count_back`. I find them clearer. But as said, it's not a big deal, it's up to you.
Looks good to me, great job!
I think the PR is great as it is, but I also agree with reduz that the `legible_unique_name` and `internal` arguments could be swapped.

> I also agree with reduz that the legible_unique_name and internal arguments could be swapped.

What? Where he said that?
Also `internal` has very little use outside core. It might be useful only for some plugins. It's better left at the very end of the argument list.

@KoBeWi
>Additionally, I am uncertain how many times legible unique name is used (I think only the editor uses it), so it may be better to swap the order of the two arguments to make this one come second.

Yep, I just saw it. `legible_unique_name` is useful when you create a new node (e.g. `Node2D.new()`) and don't want it to have random name, but also don't want to name it yourself. It can even be used during runtime, to recognize nodes on remote tree. It's not used often, but has more applications for regular user than `internal` parameter. I'd leave it as is.

EDIT:
Although considering only core use, swapping could make sense 🤔 But GDScript usage is more important.
Yeah I agree I think its better as it is now, your point of not making users pass this internal argument unnecesary makes more sense than legible unique name.

comments:
I found that this is caused because it is possible to remove default children's of node which are created by default by Godot (This also happens with AcceptDialog and others)

This nodes are created by Godot when user create only AcceptDialog
![Zrzut ekranu z 2019-07-06 18-23-46](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/41945903/60758762-4db85d00-a01b-11e9-80c2-1e52c65ab669.png)

This line cause crash:
```
for i in get_children():
    i.queue_free()
```

review_comments: The problem here is that you are assuming all internal nodes will come after but, in some situations, this is not desired (such as scrollbars above children controls in ScrollContainer). This system may work if you specify where you want internal children behind or after the user nodes, so you might need two separate arrays.

The problem here is that you are assuming all internal nodes will come after but, in some situations, this is not desired (such as scrollbars above children controls in ScrollContainer). This system may work if you specify where you want internal children behind or after the user nodes, so you might need two separate arrays.
